ideas.title: Improve Your Trading With Kaufman Indicators - Perry Kaufman And Kevin Davey
ideas.name: Efficiency ratio ranking of markets (also stated in fI3IWoTORUo)
ideas.markets: any basket of markets; Kaufman names interest-rate markets and stock-index markets as the two ends of the ranking
ideas.entry: No trade rule. Compute the efficiency ratio over a short window (Kaufman suggests about 10 bars, the shortest that spreads the values out), rank all markets, then use trend systems on the high end and mean-reversion systems on the low end. As spoken the formula is the sum of absolute bar-to-bar moves versus the net distance, but he also says a higher value means more trending, which is inconsistent; the standard form is net change divided by total path, between 0 and 1, high = trending.
ideas.exit: unstated (selection filter, not a trade rule)
ideas.filters: market selection by ER rank; no fixed threshold, ranking is relative
ideas.claimed_results: No performance numbers. Checkable claims: interest-rate markets come out as the most trending and stock-index markets as the least trending, and Kaufman says that if your ranking does not show this you have computed it wrongly. ER is said to be fractal: markets high on daily bars are also high on 60-minute bars. In Davey's 44-market test the filtered trend system had a negative average trade over all markets; Kaufman says choosing high-ER markets would have removed that problem (asserted, not shown).
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Feeds P-0084 (28-market trend portfolio, market selection) and supports the RSI(5) index-ETF book (index markets are the least trending, so mean reversion fits). Not tested before.
ideas.red_flags: Formula is garbled in the transcript, so pre-register the standard definition. The sanity check is circular as a validation. Kaufman is promoting his own signals site and the masterclass. Window choice is described as important but only 10 is suggested.
ideas.why_priority: Free daily data, near-complete rule, a stated claim we can check in an hour, and the result directly informs the queued trend portfolio and the running RSI(5) book.

ideas.title: 6 Trading Ideas Most Traders Never Test - Kaufman & Davey
ideas.name: Trend-method ranking: breakout vs moving average vs regression vs exponential average, 80-day period (supported by FjqZttnWFQs)
ideas.entry: unstated beyond an 80-day calculation period; methods named are breakout, moving average, linear regression and exponential moving average
ideas.claimed_results: Breakout does far better than every other trend method tested (teaser slide, figures not readable in the transcript) and few people use it. In the long Kaufman session he separately says the exponential average is the least effective of the trend methods, with breakout, plain moving average and linear regression all better.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Extends P-0084 (trend following on 28 ETFs). Add the four methods at the same 80-day length as extra arms, with Proteus pre-registering its own breakout and exit definitions.
ideas.red_flags: Teaser clip for a paid masterclass, rules and numbers withheld on purpose. The claim comes from one speaker's study on an unnamed market set.
ideas.why_priority: Cheap to bolt onto the queued trend portfolio and the claim is a ranking we can confirm or reject, but we would have to write the rules ourselves.

ideas.title: Perry Kaufman & Kevin Davey - Open Trading Questions & Answers
ideas.name: 200-bar price momentum as a regime filter instead of a 200-bar moving average
ideas.entry: Regime reading is the sign of today's close minus the close 200 bars ago; positive means momentum up. Davey says he does not treat this as permission to trade only long: some of his strategies short when momentum is up, and he tests both directions.
ideas.claimed_results: No numbers. His stated reason: a 200-period moving average lags too much to serve as a regime filter, whereas the 200-bar change is quicker.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Direct companion to the 200 vs 222-day MA filter on SPY (P-0082). Same data, one extra column.
ideas.red_flags: Assertion without a test shown. A 200-day change and a 200-day average are strongly correlated, so a difference may be small and the risk of reading noise is high.
ideas.why_priority: Fully specified, trivial on free daily bars, and it extends a test we have already run.

ideas.title: Improve Your Trading With Kaufman Indicators - Perry Kaufman And Kevin Davey
ideas.name: Kaufman adaptive moving average, with and without an efficiency-ratio gate, against a simple moving average
ideas.markets: Davey: E-mini S&P (360-minute bars) in the demo, then a wider basket; Kaufman: many futures and stocks
ideas.timeframe: intraday in Davey's test; Kaufman uses daily
ideas.entry: Davey's long-only test: buy when the close is above the average, sell when below; the simple-average baseline uses the same rule. Third arm: only buy when the efficiency ratio is above a threshold (threshold unstated). Kaufman's current settings: ER window 60 days instead of the original 10, and the fast end of the smoothing moved from about 2-3 days to 8; the slow end is unstated. He uses it as a plain trend follower, not a regime filter.
ideas.exit: Davey: close below the average. Kaufman: unstated beyond trend following.
ideas.filters: ER threshold (unstated), market selection by ER (see B-01)
ideas.claimed_results: On the ES example the adaptive average beat the simple one on profit, drawdown and return on account, and adding the ER gate improved a second example again. No figures given, single market and bar size. Kaufman says he has tested it over a broad range of markets and it beats moving averages.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Partial overlap with the 200 vs 222 MA test (it is a moving-average rule) and with P-0084 (trend arm).
ideas.red_flags: One-chart demo. Parameter settings differ between the two speakers. The Kaufman settings were chosen with hindsight on modern markets (he says the world changed after 2000).
ideas.why_priority: Concrete settings from the inventor and an easy comparison to a plain moving average, though the slow end and ER threshold are missing.

ideas.title: Improve Your Trading With Kaufman Indicators - Perry Kaufman And Kevin Davey
ideas.name: Kaufman filter: a volatility band around the adaptive average to cut whipsaws
ideas.timeframe: intraday: bar sizes 180, then up to 1440 minutes (five sizes)
ideas.entry: Baseline: long when the average slopes up, short when it slopes down. Filtered version: enter only when the average has moved away from its latest turning point by more than a filter amount. Filter amount per Kaufman: one standard deviation of the average's movement over 10 to 15 days (the transcript is garbled on which series the deviation is taken of).
ideas.exit: unstated (presumably reversal of the slope, unconfirmed)
ideas.filters: band width one standard deviation; ER market selection suggested by Kaufman
ideas.claimed_results: 2007 to 2025, 44 markets, five bar sizes, walk-forward, any system with fewer than 50 trades dropped. The filter removed about 58 percent of trades (also described as roughly half). Average trade was still negative across all markets with the filter on, but less negative than off. Crude example: trades fell from 289 to 104, long and short sides both improved. A counter-trend (mean-reversion) version also lost trades without improving.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Davey used 180 to 1440-minute bars; a daily-bar version is a different test but the filter logic carries over.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Related to B-04 and P-0084; not previously tested.
ideas.red_flags: Davey says the aim is to compare filter on and off, not to trade the system, because it loses money overall. The filter definition is the weakest part of the transcript.
ideas.why_priority: Good evaluation design to copy (on/off over many markets, minimum 50 trades) but the filter formula is ambiguous.

ideas.title: Algorithmic Trading Tools - Must Have!
ideas.name: Equity-curve trading: take the next trade only when the strategy equity curve is above its 20-trade average
ideas.markets: any strategy's trade list (demo used a natural gas strategy)
ideas.entry: Take the next signal only if the strategy's own cumulative trade equity is above its 20-trade simple moving average. Mirror variant: turn off when the equity curve is making new highs.
ideas.exit: unstated; trades skipped while the curve is below the average
ideas.filters: 20-trade equity average (length is adjustable in his tool)
ideas.claimed_results: The tool first judges whether filtering is likely to work; for the natural gas example it said no. The 20-trade version fell off, went flat, came back on, then went flat again after riding a decline, so it did not really work. No numbers.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Can run on the RSI(5) ETF trade lists we already have. Not tested before.
ideas.red_flags: He gave a single negative example. Equity-curve filters on mean-reversion systems often cut the rebound after a loss streak, which is the opposite of what is wanted; this should be pre-registered as an expected-fail test.
ideas.why_priority: Rule is complete and cheap, but the video's own demo says it did not work, so the value is a quick falsification.

ideas.title: Crude Oil AI Inspired Algo Trading Strategy - $96K in Walkforward Profits
ideas.name: Low-ADX short-term momentum in the direction of 200-bar momentum (crude oil)
ideas.markets: crude oil futures (CL continuous; a micro contract exists)
ideas.entry: Evaluated at the close of a bar, trade at the next bar's open. Long when ADX is below a threshold (period and threshold unstated), the close is above the previous close, the close one bar ago is above the close two bars ago, and the close is above the close 200 bars ago. Short is the mirror for the two close comparisons and the 200-bar test, with ADX still below the threshold.
ideas.exit: He mentions a couple of exits. Stated: a monthly cease-trading rule that switches the strategy off for the rest of the month after a profit or loss limit (limits unstated), and a catastrophic stop of 5,000 dollars (about 5 crude points). Anything else is in the book code, unstated.
ideas.claimed_results: Title says 96K of walk-forward profit (period unstated). About 60 to 61 percent winners, both long and short profitable at similar levels, largest loser about 6,800 dollars (larger than the 5,000 stop). Trade count fell sharply in the last 2 to 3 years, with long flat spells. Since the book release in early September 2025: one down month (November), a profitable December 2025 with 4 trades, good February and March 2026 with one trade.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Original is 120-minute bars. No free intraday history, so a daily-bar analogue on CL=F, other energy and index futures or ETFs would be a different strategy, not a replication.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: none
ideas.red_flags: ADX threshold and period hidden, so any test must sweep them, which invites overfitting. Walk-forward result presented as out-of-sample. Labelled AI inspired but nothing AI-specific is shown. Part of a book funnel; costs and slippage unstated. His own caveat: hard to trade alone because it sits out for long spells.

ideas.entry: Moving-average trend following with an optimised length; no crossover or filter detail given.

Kaufman says the best S&P average length has crept up over decades (10, then 15, then 20 days) to about 110 days now, that on the S&P faster averages lose money while slow ones make money, and that in an optimisation the short end mean-reverts and the long end trends, though only modestly. He attributes it to higher volume bringing higher volatility after 2000.

ideas.title: Perry Kaufman & Kevin Davey - Open Trading Questions & Answers
ideas.name: Enter on the signal or wait for a pullback: waiting skips the winners
ideas.markets: any systematic entry (Davey: futures, Kaufman: stocks at the open)
ideas.timeframe: intraday execution; the claim can be proxied on daily bars
ideas.entry: Compare entering at the next open after a signal with placing a limit order for a better price and waiting. Pullback depth and waiting time unstated.
ideas.claimed_results: No figures. Davey: entering on the signal matched the backtest and avoided regret. Kaufman: in the 1980s many traders waited for a pullback; the trades that did not pull back were the profitable ones, so waiting systematically misses winners and results get worse. Kaufman does allow a few minutes' wait and his own entries go in ahead of the open to avoid wide spreads.
ideas.data_needed_if_not: Daily proxy: signal day close versus limit order a set percentage below, filled only if the next day's low reaches it. Fill modelling on daily bars is optimistic; true test needs intraday data.
ideas.overlaps_what_we_have: Could be run on the RSI(5) ETF signals. Not tested before.
ideas.red_flags: Anecdote, not a test. Daily-bar limit fills overstate execution quality.
ideas.why_priority: Cheap, falsifiable and relevant to every dip-buying system, but the parameters are ours to choose.

frameworks.name: Strategy factory pipeline: walk-forward, a marked live phase, and judge filters by on versus off
frameworks.what_it_is: Davey builds each strategy with walk-forward testing (optimise only on earlier data, then apply the result to unseen data), shows the closed-trade equity curve of the walk-forward results, then tracks a separate real-time phase from a fixed date (for example since a book was written in July 2025, or from 2021 for the portfolio strategies) with a dashed marker between development and live. His filter study used 44 markets, five bar sizes, 2007 to 2025, dropped any system with under 50 trades, and compared filter on versus off rather than looking at absolute profit. He also keeps one rule across a portfolio rather than tuning per strategy. Kaufman adds: test any change over 20 or more years, not the last few, and if a system trades rarely, extend the history and replicate on similar markets (corn on soybeans and wheat, one index on others).
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Add a walk-forward harness to the probe loop, set an automatic 50-trade minimum, report every filter as an on-versus-off delta over the full 28-market set, and treat the commit timestamp as the start of the live phase. Note the caveat: a walk-forward curve is still developed data, so only post-commit results count as out-of-sample.

frameworks.name: Live versus ideal reconciliation and divergence alerts
frameworks.what_it_is: Plot the real account equity against the strategy engine's idealised equity on one chart. They drift because of missed, delayed or rejected orders, and he wants the real line at or above the ideal one. In another video he says he had AI write code that emails him when the strategy's number and the real number diverge. He also shows individual strategy curves next to the portfolio curve, and the losing months.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Extend audit/recompute.js so every night it compares the paper-trade ledger with an ideal signal replay and writes an alert line (and a Field Notes item) on divergence. Show the monthly return table including losing months on the lab page.

frameworks.name: Portfolio assembly: weekly correlation table, constant sizing, keep weak but uncorrelated strategies
frameworks.what_it_is: An equity curve combiner reads weekly returns of several strategies, draws the combined curve with a dashed line where out-of-sample starts, and prints a correlation matrix (his five demo strategies were near zero and two natural gas strategies were only about 0.1 apart). In the portfolio videos he covers six of seven futures sectors, trades one contract each so growth is not flattered by scaling size, and argues a strategy that loses money alone may still help by earning when the others lose.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Compute weekly return correlations across the nine-ETF RSI(5) book and the P-0084 portfolio, plot constant-unit curves, and test whether dropping the weakest standalone arm helps or hurts drawdown.

frameworks.name: Metric validation against forward results
frameworks.what_it_is: Do not discard a strategy because one metric looks bad (you can always find one) and do not borrow metrics from books. Pick the backtest metrics that you have shown correlate with later live performance. Davey says he did this over real-money history and found some metrics did not matter; he still uses net profit as his walk-forward objective despite the standard advice against it. No data is shown.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: With 80 or more probes, tabulate in-sample metrics (profit factor, win rate, drawdown, trade count) against forward outcome and pre-register which ones PASS-MARKS use. Treat his claim as unverified until our own table supports it.

frameworks.name: Where AI belongs and where it does not
frameworks.what_it_is: Fine uses: idea generation, feature ideas (turn off after a profit run), data cleaning (spotting decimal-point errors in highs), porting code between platforms, researching an economic rationale, analysing trade timing, writing monitoring scripts, and cross-auditing calculations with two different models. Not fine: letting AI set position sizing or risk limits, optimise parameters, run build and validation end to end, or design the portfolio. A specific trap: if AI finds a pattern or rationale on all your data and you then test on the same data, you have used the data twice.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Proteus is the case he warns about, so keep humans-in-charge items in code (pre-registered pass marks, permutation test, risk limits in CHARTER.md). Run a data sanity pass on Yahoo bars before each test, record which data the idea-finder saw, and have a second model recompute headline numbers.

frameworks.name: Quit rules and the quit game
frameworks.what_it_is: A library of standard rules for when to stop trading a strategy, replayed on out-of-sample curves, a portfolio version that picks one rule for all strategies, and an interactive game that reveals a hidden live curve step by step, asks you where you would quit, and scores that against the best risk-adjusted exit and the nearest standard rule. He found his own habit matched quitting at the second significant drawdown. He does not include restart rules, noting that it is psychologically hard to resume a strategy after it has just recovered.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: See B-05. The psychology half does not apply to an agent, but a pre-registered quit and restart rule per desk does.

frameworks.name: Fix the side and the sizing before seeing results
frameworks.what_it_is: Davey's ES strategy loses on the short side. His position: dropping the short side after seeing that is optimising by another route; decide long-only or long and short at the start. The same logic: do not pick the best position-sizing method per strategy, and do not assume a regime means longs only; test both sides.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Already close to Proteus practice. Make the direction and sizing choices explicit lines in every probe's pre-registration so they cannot be changed after the first result.

frameworks.name: Shadow log for discretion and know your engine's quirks
frameworks.what_it_is: If you want to override a system, log what you did next to what the system would have done and judge the override over time, including the mental cost. Both speakers say the best software is the one you know well enough to see how it can give false results, test daily systems on 1-minute bars when stops and limits are involved, and prefer uncleaned intraday data because live feeds contain bad ticks.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: Keep a do-nothing shadow for any paper trade Luke or a child overrides. For daily tests, write down the fill assumptions (open, close, limit) in each probe note.

frameworks.name: Pre-committed plan for drawdowns
frameworks.what_it_is: In his contests Davey set up his plan to aim for 100 percent or blow the account. One year he started at 15,000 and was down about 50 percent after roughly three months, which was within the plan, and then months of nothing followed. Multiple 30 percent drawdowns and flat years happened even in the three winning years. His point is to prepare mentally for the worst case and keep to the plan.
frameworks.how_proteus_could_use_it: For the supercar target, write the acceptable drawdown and the stop line down before the first trade, with the sequence of long flat spells in mind.
